conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Morales, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My job is to check in on how moms are feeling in the weeks and months after birth, because the emotional changes that ride along with new motherhood are just as important as the physical ones.

I’ll be using a short questionnaire called the EPDS—short for Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. It’s simply ten questions about your mood and thoughts over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want the most honest snapshot of how you’ve been feeling so we know how best to support you. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team unless you tell us something that makes us worry about your immediate safety, in which case we’d talk together about the next steps.

We’ll go through one question at a time. I’ll ask it conversationally—no need to remember any numbers—and we’ll move at your pace. Ready to start?

First, thinking about the past week: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that been difficult for you?

Honestly, I’ve really struggled to laugh lately. My husband tried to joke about the baby’s 3 a.m. “performances” and I just stared at him. I used to laugh at his silly impressions, but this week even the cutest things feel flat. I’ll force a little smile so he doesn’t worry, but it feels forced—like I’m just going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wish I could say that. Most days nothing feels funny. I see other people laugh and I think, “I should be laughing too,” but the moment just passes me by.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk around the lake, even just binge-watching a show. Now when I think about doing any of that, it feels like one more chore. I still go through the motions so I don’t seem “off,” but inside it’s flat, like someone dimmed the lights on everything I used to like.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing. When he wouldn’t settle last night, I kept replaying whether I missed his sleepy cues. I even apologized to my mom for the state of the living room—like a messy house makes me a bad mom. The rational part of me knows babies just cry and laundry piles up, but the guilt still barges in and parks itself on my chest.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s not getting enough milk—even though the pediatrician says he’s gaining fine. Or I’ll lie down and picture the binky falling on the floor and him somehow choking on it later. I know the chances are tiny, but I still check the monitor every five minutes. It’s like my brain’s stuck on “what-if” and won’t turn off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

That happens too—especially in the evenings. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight, my hands feel shaky, and I’m convinced something awful is about to happen, even when everything’s quiet. It’s like an alarm goes off inside me, but there’s no real danger I can point to. After a while it fades, but it leaves me exhausted and on edge, waiting for the next wave.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most days. Between feeding every couple of hours, trying to catch a nap before he wakes, and the pile of laundry that never shrinks, it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. Some mornings I just sit on the couch staring at the mess, wondering how I’ll get through the next hour, let alone the whole week. I usually manage the basics eventually, but it’s like walking through quicksand—everything takes ten times the effort it used to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, I’ll finally get him down and crawl into bed, but then my head starts spinning—did I wash the bottles, is he still breathing, am I already failing him? Some nights I just lie there wide-awake until the sky turns pale, even when the baby’s sleeping a three-hour stretch. When I do drift off, I jerk awake at every squeak over the monitor. It’s like my body forgot how to let go and rest.
I have felt sad or miserable

That pretty much sums up the week. It’s not tears every second, more like a gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel this heaviness in my chest, like I’m sinking. I keep telling myself I should be grateful—he’s healthy, I’ve got support—but the sadness just sits there, dull and stubborn, and I can’t shake it off.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah... it’s happened a few times. Yesterday I cried in the shower because I couldn’t get the stroller unfolded fast enough for our walk. The day before, I just looked at the baby’s tiny socks and the tears started. It’s not loud sobbing—more like this quiet leak I can’t seem to turn off. I try to hide it so my older daughter doesn’t see, but sometimes I wake up and realize the pillow’s already damp.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless at times, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. Really, I just want to feel like myself again so I can be the mom my kids deserve.

I hear how hard these first weeks have been for you. The joy you once found in small, everyday pleasures-laughing with your husband, looking forward to a walk-feels distant, replaced by a heavy gray cloud and constant worry about whether you're doing everything "right." You're exhausted yet unable to rest, overwhelmed by tasks that used to feel simple, and crying over things that shouldn't bring tears. Still, you're fighting to keep going for your children, and that strength matters.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports complete inability to find things funny, matching 'Not at all</sym>, <sym>"Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, excessive self-blame occurring "all the time" across multiple routine situations, matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries, constant scanning of monitor, and uncontrollable 'what-if' thinking—clearly 'very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms and dread, happening "quite a lot" without identifiable triggers.</sym>, <sym>Response shows frequent overwhelm ('most days') and significant functional impact ('walking through quicksand'), aligning with 'sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by anxious intrusive thoughts, inability to fall asleep for hours, and frequent awakenings despite baby sleeping—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Response conveys near-constant low mood with persistent heaviness and inability to feel relief, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Multiple recent episodes (yesterday, day before) with spontaneous onset and persistent damp pillow indicate crying "quite often".</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 25 on the EPDS places well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>postpartum depression</med>. Your responses map to five+ key symptoms of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with peripartum onset</med>: markedly diminished interest or pleasure (anhedonia), significant weight or appetite change implied by feeling depleted, sleep disturbance, psychomotor agitation described as "heart racing", fatigue and worthlessness/guilt ("like I'm already failing him"), diminished ability to think or concentrate (mind "spinning"), and recurrent tearfulness. Associated <sym>anxiety symptoms</sym>-daily free-floating worry, nocturnal hyper-vigilance, sudden panic with chest tightness-commonly co-occur in the perinatal period and intensify distress. Protective factor: no self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> to discuss results and consider therapy or medication options
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for comprehensive evaluation and evidence-based treatment
3. Reach out today to a trusted friend, partner, or relative-share how low you're feeling so you have practical help with baby care and household tasks
4. Practice 15-20 minutes of protected rest when baby sleeps; let non-essential chores wait-recovery is the priority
5. Use calming strategies when panic rises: slow diaphragmatic breathing, grounding by naming five things you can see/hear/feel, or brief progressive muscle relaxation
6. Consider joining a local or online new-mom support group; hearing others' stories can reduce isolation
7. Keep the 24-hr <med>Postpartum Support International</med> helpline number 1-800-944-4773 (text 800-944-4773, English/Español) in your phone for immediate support
8. Return for EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks or sooner if mood worsens, panic increases, or any thoughts of self-harm emerge
9. Schedule pediatric follow-up to reinforce baby's wellbeing and ease milk-supply worries; bring partner or support person to appointments
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS responses):
- Marked anhedonia: loss of humor, anticipatory enjoyment, and interest in previously pleasurable activities
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” frequent crying spells (out of proportion to triggers)
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care and household tasks
- Daily, intrusive “what-if” anxiety, physiologic panic symptoms (tight chest, racing heart, tremor), worse in evenings
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed/drowning in routine tasks; tasks feel like “walking through quicksand”
- Sleep disturbance: initial insomnia and hyper-vigilance even when infant sleeps; frequent nocturnal awakenings
- No current self-harm ideation; protective factor: strong motivation “to feel like myself again” for children

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days,” duration ≥ past week, interfere with functioning and rest.

Screening significance: High endorsement of depressive and anxiety items consistent with possible postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; score interpretation suggests elevated risk requiring further evaluation.

Safety: Denies suicidal or self-harm thoughts; no plan or intent. Continue to monitor.

Next step: Recommend formal assessment with standardized tool (EPDS total score) and clinician interview; consider referral for perinatal mental health services.
